doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: First European tour in 1952-53, Sweden and a demanding promoter
summary: Overseas with Louis: a town that closed for the concert, then a German promoter rushing the band.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You got to go overseas with Louis’ and other groups too?
Well the other group was with Peanuts Hucko.
Was there certain places that you’ve played that were particularly memorable overseas?

Mostly all the places because especially, like I say, I wrote everything down. So I remember every place. One of the most exhilarating experiences was when we got to Switzerland, the first time I played in Switzerland. The first time I went into Europe with Louis was in October of 1952. ’52 or ’53. What? You don’t remember?

Yeah the first place was Sweden, and we got into this town and the place was closed. There wasn’t a thing in town. I met a guy and he could speak English and he spoke to me, “you with Louis Armstrong?” I says, “hey where is everybody?” He says, “what do you mean?” “I don’t see anybody in the streets, nobody walking, the shops are closing.” He says, “Louis Armstrong’s here.” I said, “what do you mean?” He said, “they closed the whole town,” they were getting prepared to go see Louis at the concert. I swear to God, man. He said, “what do you mean, Louis Armstrong’s here.” I said oh, okay. So anyway it was Sweden, then we went to Denmark, then we were here and we traveled a lot, but it was so rough I’m telling you. Because we were doing not only like we’d play one country here today and then go to the next country, we would play two shows, one in the afternoon and one in the evening and sometimes a second one would even be in a different country. We got to Germany and this promoter, she was money hungry, she was trying to get as much out of Louis as she could. And we got to a town, I forget where it was, it might have been Munich, and we check into the hotel and we were so tired, because we had just gotten off a bus about 13 hours or so. And we checked in about 7:30 or quarter to 8. And 8:15 she was downstairs, “let’s go, the concert’s at 8:30.” We had to

get back on the bus. And we just had time to put your bags down, wash your face, shave, and run downstairs. So I went past the dining room, and Arvell Shaw was sitting in the dining room. And I said how are we going to eat? He says, “man I’ve got to get something, I’m starving, I’m just having some soup.” I said, “I’m going to do that too.” So I sat down with him and I ordered some soup. So now here comes Louis walking past the dining room and we were sitting right by the door, the entrance. He says, “hey man, what you guys doing?” We said we’ve got to have something. He went “yeah I’m going to have some too.” Next thing you know the whole band was sitting at our table. And she came, she was fuming. She was ranting and screaming, and Louis told her all kinds of words. I mean we’ve got to eat something, we’re starving man, we’re hungry, we’ll do your concerts. Well you know how they are. Concert says 8:30, we’ve got to start at 8:30. It was crazy. So we all ate and we said get lost. And next thing you know a guy says I’ll have a steak or give me a sandwich, and Louis says bring me some of this. So he says that’s it man, get lost, get out. She was crazy man. But I’ll tell you I don’t know how Louis did it. You know how he did it? He loved it. Well of course his biggest thrill was being in front of people because he would always say those people came to see me, I’m going to do the best that I can do, which is very admirable, right?
